newsitem.title: USA: Du Pont jury rehears testimony.
newsitem.headline: Du Pont jury rehears testimony.

text.p: Jurors in the John du Pont murder trial entered their fourth day of deliberations on Friday by revisiting testimony from eyewitnesses who said they saw him kill Olympic champion wrestler David Schultz.
The jurors appeared to be focusing on the moments before and immediately after the killing to determine what degree of homicide was applicable under Pennsylvania law.

Prosecutors told reporters on Friday any continued deadlock that led to a hung jury would be viewed with displeasure. "We would be displeased," said Joe Grace, assistant Delaware County district attorney, when asked about the prospect of a hung jury.

Since beginning their deliberations Tuesday afternoon, jurors have repeatedly returned to the courtroom to hear rereadings of testimony or jury instructions dealing with the three degrees of homicide du Pont has been charged with.

On Friday morning, they heard a rereading of testimony from Schutlz's widow, Nancy, and Patrick Goodale, a du Pont security consultant who accompanied the millionaire chemicals heir to Schultz's home on the day of the killing, Jan. 26, 1996.
Schultz was killed outside his home on the du Pont estate, where he worked as a coach at a training facility du Pont established.

Both witnesses described du Pont shooting Schultz without warning after du Pont drove up to Schultz's driveway. They described du Pont aiming a third shot into Schultz as the wrestler lay face down, motionless in the snow.

In addition, Goodale said in his testimony, du Pont asked Schultz "you got a problem with me?" after firing the first shot into Schultz's chest. Prosecutors have argued that this comment indicated du Pont acted out of anger and resentment toward Schultz.
Du Pont's lawyers have conceded du Pont killed Schultz, but they are seeking a verdict of not guilty by reason of insanity.
In addition to verdicts of not guilty or not guilty by reason of insanity, the jurors can render verdicts of guilty or guilty but mentally ill.

However, jurors may have moved beyond the insanity issue. On Thursday, they asked Court of Common Pleas Judge Patricia Jenkins to reread for them, twice over, definitions of the three degrees of homicide du Pont has been charged with.
They are first degree murder, third degree murder, and voluntary manslaughter.

The essential differences between the degrees are that first-degree murder requires both a specific intent to kill and legal malice to convict, third degree requires malice only, and voluntary manslaughter requires a mistaken belief that circumstances that would justify a killing existed.
The jurors also asked for a repeat of the definition of legal malice, which Jenkins described as an intent to kill or cause serious bodily injury, or extreme indifference to human life.
